Reference: ETH-002-10-2026

October 2026

Summary: Humanitarian situation in Tigray, covering displacement, livelihoods, access to essential services, humanitarian assistance and movement restrictions, including the impact of renewed fighting in 2026.

Summary

Tigray continues to face a severe humanitarian situation due to the lasting effects of the 2020–2022 conflict, renewed fighting in 2026, prolonged displacement, climatic shocks and disrupted livelihoods. Essential services and humanitarian assistance remain available, but their coverage, accessibility and reliability vary. The available evidence indicates that conditions vary by location and population group.

In general, the humanitarian situation in Tigray is not so severe that there are substantial grounds for believing there is a real risk of serious harm because conditions amount to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment as defined in paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iii) of the Immigration Rules/Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).

Even where there is not, in general, a real risk of serious harm because of the general humanitarian situation, a person may still face a real risk of serious harm because of their specific circumstances. Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

When considering this, decision makers should note the Upper Tribunal (UT)’s findings and general approach to assessing humanitarian conditions in OA (Somalia) (CG) [2022] UKUT 33 (IAC) (2 February 2022):

‘In an Article 3 “living conditions” case, there must be a causal link between the Secretary of State’s removal decision and any “intense suffering” feared by the returnee. This includes a requirement for temporal proximity between the removal decision and any “intense suffering” of which the returnee claims to be at real risk. This reflects the requirement in Paposhvili [2017] Imm AR 867 for intense suffering to be “serious, rapid and irreversible” in order to engage the returning State’s obligations under Article 3 ECHR. A returnee fearing “intense suffering” on account of their prospective living conditions at some unknown point in the future is unlikely to be able to attribute responsibility for those living conditions to the Secretary of State, for to do so would be speculative.’ (Headnote 1)

‘… There will need to be a careful assessment of all the circumstances of the particular individual in order to ascertain the Article 3, humanitarian protection or internal relocation implications of an individual’s return.’ (Headnote 12).

Based on the findings in OA, the threshold for granting humanitarian protection under paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iii) of the Immigration Rules in an Article 3 ECHR “living conditions” case is very high. Applying these findings in relation to Tigray, the onus is on the person to demonstrate that they would be unable to obtain food, water, accommodation and other essentials on return (including through their support networks and any financial assistance) and that this would cause intense suffering which would be ‘serious, rapid and irreversible.’

When determining this, decision makers must carefully consider the person’s individual circumstances. These include, but are not limited to, factors such as gender, age, marital status, dependants (e.g. children), work experience/skills, financial savings, remittances, and medical conditions. Conditions are particularly challenging for internally displaced persons (IDPs), IDP returnees and in the contested areas disputed between Tigray and Amhara (see Conditions in IDP settlements and for IDP returnees). Another key consideration is whether the person will have access to a support network upon return that could help them to meet their basic needs. Humanitarian aid organisations operate in Tigray but are unable to reach all of those in need, leading them to prioritise those with the most severe needs (see Humanitarian assistance).

Internal relocation is location- and person-specific. Relocation is possible to Addis Ababa and Mekelle. Relocation is unlikely to be reasonable to contested areas and those undergoing active hostilities. The reasonableness of relocation must be assessed on the facts of the individual case.

All cases must be considered on their individual facts, with the onus on the person to demonstrate they face persecution or serious harm.

Displacement remains substantial in Tigray. Although approximately 1.12 million IDPs had returned to their areas of origin, around 761,000 people remained internally displaced as of August 2026, with many, particularly those from contested areas, unable to return. IDPs and returnees continue to face difficulties accessing adequate shelter, livelihoods, healthcare, education and other essential services (see Forced population displacement, IDP returns and Conditions in IDP settlements and for IDP returnees).

Economic recovery remains limited, with employment below the national average and cash, fuel and salary shortages reducing households’ ability to afford essentials (see Economy).

Food insecurity and malnutrition remain significant, particularly among IDPs, returnees and households in drought- and conflict-affected areas. In January 2026, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) assessed that some households in Tigray, especially IDPs in camps, were likely experiencing at least household-level Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes, indicating food consumption gaps or an ability to meet minimum food needs only through depletion of livelihood assets or crisis coping strategies. Separately, The New Humanitarian reported in October 2026 that a September overview by the Tigray Disaster Risk Management Commission estimated that 3.9 million people required emergency food assistance (Access to food).

Essential services remain available, but their accessibility, affordability and reliability are constrained. The Ethiopian government reported that by the end of 2023, nearly all hospitals and health centres and over 90% of health posts in Tigray had been restored. However, shortages of medicines, supplies, fuel and staff, high medical costs and conflict related disruptions continue to hamper access and service delivery (see Access to health). The Global Education Cluster recorded approximately 1.35 million children out of school as of November 2025. Ethiopian Ministry of Education data for 2024/25 showed enrolment ratios below national levels for pre-primary and Grades 1–8, but above national levels for Grades 9–12 (see Access to education). An estimated 54% of Tigray’s population has access to basic drinking water, broadly similar to the national level of 57%. However, access to basic sanitation is substantially lower, at 10.4% compared with 31% nationally (see Access to WASH). Displacement and return assessments describe inadequate and overcrowded shelter and damaged or destroyed homes (see Access to shelter). UN agencies, national and international NGOs provide humanitarian assistance but is not sufficient or accessible to everyone in need. Insecurity, ongoing violence, funding constraints, fuel and cash shortages, movement restriction, disruptions in banking and telecommunications, constrain operations and access (see Humanitarian assistance and Freedom of movement).

Country information

About this bulletin

This standalone bulletin focuses on the humanitarian situation in Tigray, including economic conditions, displacement, access to food, healthcare, education, water and sanitation, shelter, humanitarian assistance, and freedom of movement. It examines the impact of ongoing insecurity, displacement, climatic shocks, and service disruptions on the civilian population. The bulletin considers developments between 2025 and October 2026, including the humanitarian consequences of renewed fighting in 2026 and the continuing effects of conflict-related displacement and service disruption.

The COI provides the basis for the assessment. Decision makers must use relevant COI as the evidential basis for decisions.

The cut-off date for COI included in this bulletin is 22 October 2026.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents COI, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Economy

1.1 Overview

1.1.1 A March 2026 report by the Rift Valley Institute, an independent, non-profit research organisation whose work focuses on political, social, economic and security issues in eastern and central Africa[footnote 1] (RVI March 2026 report) noted that Tigray’s economy had not fully recovered from the destruction caused by the 2020–2022 conflict, with markets and farms continuing to be affected in early 2026. RVI reported extremely high unemployment, particularly among demobilised youth, which it linked to illegal mining, smuggling, banditry, migration, and vulnerability to recruitment into insurgencies and political violence. It further noted that clashes between the TDF and ENDF in January and February 2026 contributed to rising prices for essential goods and a severe cash shortage. RVI characterised the continuing situation in Tigray as a human security crisis marked by hunger, unemployment, fear, migration, and damaged infrastructure[footnote 2].

1.1.2 In March 2026, the Global Protection Cluster, a humanitarian coordination body responsible for coordinating protection activities for people affected by conflict, displacement, disasters and other emergencies[footnote 3], reported a further decline in fuel supplies and a shortage of physical cash in banks, resulting in daily queues. The report noted that banks were reportedly providing a maximum of ETB 1,000 (£4.63[footnote 4]) or less per day, and that cash was often unavailable which affected humanitarian interventions[footnote 5].

1.1.3 On 24 August 2026 Addis Standard reported:

‘The Tigray Finance and Resource Cooperation Bureau has warned that an 8.5 billion [£39.38 million[footnote 6]] birr budget shortfall has plunged the region into a severe financial crisis, disrupting salary payments for civil servants and halting development projects, according to a formal letter sent to Ethiopia’s Ministry of Finance.

‘In the letter, the bureau said funds expected to be disbursed between October and March have not been released, creating “an acute fiscal pressure that is affecting core government functions” across the region …

‘The bureau said the funding gap has made it impossible to pay salaries for more than 141,000 civil servants …

‘According to the bureau, the budget disruption has also affected development spending, with more than 844 million birr [£3.91million[footnote 7]] allocated for development objectives yet to be disbursed, while over 20 major projects across the region have reportedly stalled due to lack of funding.

‘The letter said that under the 2018 Ethiopian fiscal year budget, Tigray was allocated 23.6 billion birr [£109.33 million[footnote 8]] with 17.1 billion birr [£79.22 million[footnote 9]] expected to have been transferred by March. However, the region said it has so far received only 8.5 billion birr [£0.03 billion[footnote 10]], roughly half of the expected disbursement for the period.’[footnote 11]

1.1.4 According to an April 2026 article by Eurafrica Press & News, an online news and analysis platform reporting on political, economic and security issues in Africa and Europe[footnote 12], Tigray’s post-war economic recovery remained largely stalled three years after the Pretoria Agreement. The report cited business representatives as describing severe shortages of cash and finance, limited access to credit, fuel shortages and a lack of reconstruction, with much of the war-damaged industrial base remaining non-operational. It noted that factories which had previously been major employers and contributors to exports had not resumed normal operations. According to the report industry accounted for 26.3% of Tigray’s regional GDP in 2016/17, but that the sector’s contribution had fallen to an estimated 2% to 3% following the conflict due to destruction, displacement and stalled recovery. Business representatives interviewed by the report attributed continuing economic difficulties to both war-related damage and ongoing political instability, which they said had hindered economic recovery and investment[footnote 13].

1.2 Employment

1.2.1 The June 2026 Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (EDHS) report based on data collected between 1 August 2024 and 14 April 2025[footnote 14] (ESS EDHS 2024/25 June 2026 report) stated that 41% of women aged 15–49 and 87% of men were currently employed nationally. In Tigray 37.5% of women and 79.6% of men were employed[footnote 15].

1.2.2 The September 2026 Ethiopia Statistical Services (ESS) key findings report of the National Integrated Household Survey (ESS NIHS September 2026 report) stated the employment to population ratio in Tigray was 52.7%, compared with 61.3% nationally. Employment rates were lower for both men and women in Tigray than nationally, with 63.7% of men and 42.7% of women employed, compared with national rates of 71.8% and 50.9% respectively[footnote 16].

1.2.3 In terms of numbers, the same source indicated that in Tigray, 88.0% of the economically active population was employed, equivalent to 2,184,319 people out of 2,480,972 economically active individuals. Employment was concentrated in rural areas, where 1,561,862 people were employed, compared with 622,458 in urban areas. [The rural and urban employment figures sum to 2,184,320, one more than the source’s reported total of 2,184,319. Figures are reproduced as published]. Nationally, the employment rate among the economically active population was slightly higher at 90.4%, with 49,093,745 people employed out of an economically active population of 54,331,979[footnote 17].

1.3 Unemployment

1.3.1 The ESS EDHS 2024-5 June 2026 report noted that 55.8% of women and 14.5% of men in Tigray had not been employed during the 12 months preceding the survey[footnote 18]. Nationally, the corresponding figures were 50% for women and 8% for men[footnote 19].

1.3.2 The ESS NIHS September 2026 survey data indicated that Tigray accounted for approximately 5.7% of the country’s unemployed population (296,653 out of 5.24 million unemployed persons nationally) in 2024/25[footnote 20]. The data also showed that unemployment in Tigray was proportionately higher than the national average. Tigray’s unemployment rate stood at 12.0%, compared with 9.6% nationally. The data further indicated that Tigray had the third-highest unemployment rate among Ethiopia’s regions, behind Addis Ababa (19.1%) and Dire Dawa (14.5%), and above other large regions such as Oromia (10.5%)[footnote 21].

1.3.3 The same source noted that the female unemployment rate in Tigray was 12.5%, compared with 11.2% for males. Nationally, female unemployment was similar, at 12.8%, but male unemployment was lower, at 7.2%[footnote 22]. Youth unemployment in Tigray was 16.3%, compared with 12.9% nationally, the third-highest regional rate after Addis Ababa (20.3%) and Dire Dawa (17.7%). Oromia (14.4%) and Somali (13.1%) also recorded rates above the national average [footnote 23]. Unlike the national pattern, where female youth unemployment (17.4%) was almost twice the male rate (9.1%), youth unemployment in Tigray was broadly similar for young men (16.9%) and women (15.6%), with both rates exceeding the national average[footnote 24].

1.3.4 The ESS September 2026 report reported that unemployment was consistently higher in urban areas than in rural areas throughout Ethiopia. Nationally, urban unemployment stood at 17.2%, compared with 7.4% in rural areas. In Tigray, the urban-rural divide was particularly pronounced among young people. Youth unemployment in urban areas reached 23.0%, compared with 12.8% in rural areas, a gap of more than 10 percentage points. Tigray’s urban youth unemployment rate was also higher than the national urban average of 20.6%, while its rural youth unemployment rate exceeded the national rural average of 10.2%[footnote 25].

2. Security situation

2.1.1 For information on outbreak of conflict, geographic spread and extent of fighting see BLTN ETH: Tigray security situation.

3. Impact of conflict on civilians

3.1 Civilian targeting

3.1.1 On 10 September 2026, the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect (GCR2P), an international NGO that conducts research and advocacy on the prevention of genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity[footnote 26], published a statement by several civil society organisations expressing grave concern over escalating violence, instability and mass atrocity crimes across Ethiopia. It stated:

‘In Tigray, communities are once again facing the risk of large-scale conflict as violence escalates and prospects for de-escalation diminish. Fighting between the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and Tigrayan forces resumed on 1 August, and the government has reportedly launched near-daily drone strikes in Tigray since then, including attacks affecting civilians and civilian infrastructure such as schools, river banks, farms and residential homes. The renewed fighting has also reportedly forced hundreds of civilians to flee into Sudan. These developments follow earlier government drone attacks in January 2026, as well as troop mobilizations and clashes.’[footnote 27]

3.1.2 A 25 September 2026, OHCHR press release stated: ‘UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk on Friday expressed alarm at the widening impact of the escalating fighting in Ethiopia on civilians. Airstrikes by the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), some carried out using drones, reportedly hit five schools in Tigray on 22 September, resulting in deaths and injuries. A mortar strike on 23 September in Kobo town in Amhara reportedly by the ENDF also resulted in civilian deaths.’[footnote 28]

3.1.3 On 25 September 2026, HRW reported that an apparent Ethiopian government airstrike struck a residential compound in the Daero neighbourhood of Mekelle on 20 August 2026. HRW reported that residents and witnesses said there were no Tigrayan fighters or other military personnel present at the compound or in the surrounding area. HRW further stated that it found no evidence to support reports that the attack was intended to target nearby Tigrayan military or civilian leaders. Victims were taken to Ayder Referral Hospital, where medical staff reported treating 13 people for injuries sustained in the strike[footnote 29].

3.1.4 On 28 September 2026, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) reported a sharp increase in conflict-related casualties following the resumption of fighting between TPLF-aligned forces and the ENDF. According to MSF, the number of war-wounded patients treated at hospitals in Korem and Alamata rose from around 180 within a 48-hour period to more than 420 between 22 and 25 September 2026. In north-western Tigray, more than 300 war-wounded patients had arrived at Suhul Hospital in Shire by 25 September. MSF also suspended its activities at Alamata Hospital due to the security situation and redeployed staff to hospitals receiving large numbers of wounded patients[footnote 30]​.

3.1.5 On 30 September 2026, BBC reported that hospital sources stated that at least 52 civilians were killed during three days of fighting in and around Alamata. A doctor at Alamata General Hospital told the BBC that heavy explosives and artillery were used during the fighting, some of which struck residential areas. The doctor stated that those killed included children, mothers and cattle herders, and that 12 people were killed in a strike on the town’s marketplace. Separately, MSF reported that more than 700 war-wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supported in Tigray[footnote 31].

3.1.6 The Armed Conflict Location and Events Data Project (ACLED) provides information on civilian targeting. ACLED defines civilian targeting as ‘events in which civilians were the main or only target of an event’[footnote 32]. Between 1 January and 4 October 2026, ACLED recorded 52 civilian-targeting events in Tigray, resulting in 14 reported fatalities. The highest number of incidents was recorded in Southern Tigray (18 events; 5 fatalities) and Central Tigray (16 events; 1 fatality). North Western Tigray recorded fewer incidents (8 events) but the highest number of fatalities (8). Mekelle (6 events), Eastern Tigray (2 events), and South Eastern (2 events) recorded no associated fatalities[footnote 33]. Civilian-targeting events do not encompass all civilian casualties in conflict.

3.1.7 ACLED also recorded violence against civilians defined ‘as events where an organised armed group inflicts violence on unarmed non-combatants.’ It includes attempted or actual physical harm and forced disappearance. Its sub-event types are ‘Attack,’ ‘Abduction/forced disappearance’ and Sexual violence’[footnote 34]. Between 1 January and 4 October 2026, ACLED reported 43 incidents of violence against civilians resulting in 6 fatalities. These consisted of abductions/forced disappearances (29 events; no fatalities), attacks (11 events; 6 fatalities) and sexual violence (3 events; no fatalities). ACLED attributed all but 3 events of violence against civilians to the TDF[footnote 35]. ACLED also reported 10 conflict related arrest events of which the TDF was responsible for 5, the Tigray state police for 4 events and Kebele community police for one[footnote 36].

4. Humanitarian situation

4.1 Overview and people in need of humanitarian assistance

4.1.1 The European Commission noted on its Ethiopia webpage: ‘As in 2025, there are no updated official figures on the number of people in need in Ethiopia in 2026 due to the lack of agreed humanitarian analysis with the authorities. The last official figures available date back to 2024, where there were 21.4 million people in need of humanitarian aid, with 15.8 million in need of food assistance.’[footnote 37]

4.1.2 UNICEF noted in its 2026 funding appeal:

‘Ethiopia is facing a deepening crisis driven by ongoing conflict, climate shocks and public health emergencies. Humanitarian needs are expected to rise in 2026, particularly as conflict persists in regions including Amhara, Oromia and Tigray. In Tigray, the projected return of more than 500,000 people to their places of origin in Western Tigray will take place in a context of severely disrupted basic services. Hundreds of thousands of internally displaced persons remain in overcrowded camps with limited access to essential services, and the situation in Western Tigray remains particularly complex and sensitive. Adults and children with disabilities in Ethiopia face heightened vulnerabilities due to stigma, discrimination and limited access to services. The 2025 national disability survey found that 20 per cent of households include a person with a disability, with the highest prevalence in Tigray (30 per cent).

‘In 2026, UNICEF is appealing for $401.5 million to address the most critical humanitarian needs of children, women and men affected by multiple and overlapping shocks in Ethiopia. This funding will support urgent humanitarian assistance for 8.9 million people, including 6.3 million children.’[footnote 38]

4.1.3 A March 2026 analytical report by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA), Sweden’s government agency for development cooperation[footnote 39] observed:

‘Ethiopia is one of the most complex humanitarian crises in Africa, with needs driven by multiple conflicts, disease outbreaks, worsening socioeconomic conditions and climate-related shocks such as floods and droughts. The crisis is multi-sectoral and affects most parts of the country, with overlapping needs including, protection, health, education, water, sanitation and hygiene, food security and nutrition. There are pockets of hard-to-reach populations in a few regions, especially Amhara and so-called contested areas between Amhara and Tigray, due to security risks for aid workers. Whilst the overall figure of people in need has not been officially published for almost two years, Sida estimates that 15.5 million people are in need of humanitarian aid.’[footnote 40]

4.1.4 The same source added regarding Tigray:

‘Despite the signing of Cessation of Hostilities (CoHA) in November 2022, the situation in Tigray remains dire for millions of people due to limited access to basic services, disruptions of livelihoods, and displacements. The reconstruction and rehabilitation plan for the region is severely underfunded and there is a need to restore trust in the judicial system. Humanitarian organisations have limited access to disputed areas between Tigray and Amhara, and border areas where Eritrean forces are allegedly still present. Meanwhile, internal conflicts and ethnic tensions continue to cause displacements and protection risks in other parts of the country.’[footnote 41]

4.1.5 UNICEF reported in August 2026 that, during the first six months of 2026, Ethiopia continued to face a complex humanitarian crisis driven by conflict, climate-related shocks, disease outbreaks and economic challenges. Tigray was among the regions where insecurity, violence, climatic stresses and public health emergencies exacerbated humanitarian needs, contributing to displacement, increased food insecurity and significant disruptions to essential services. According to the report, many affected communities experienced difficulties accessing safe drinking water, healthcare, adequate shelter and education. Vulnerable populations, including the urban poor and historically underserved communities, continued to face gaps in essential services, livelihood opportunities and social protection. UNICEF noted that millions of people across Ethiopia remained in urgent need of humanitarian assistance, including support relating to food security, nutrition, health, protection, education, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and emergency shelter and non-food items[footnote 42].

4.1.6 Similarly, WHO reported in August 2026, that renewed insecurity in Tigray was disrupting livelihoods, restricting humanitarian access and increasing displacement. The organisation further stated that food and nutrition insecurity were worsening during the June to September lean season, while humanitarian operations remained constrained by significant funding gaps[footnote 43].

4.1.7 The August 2026 Ethiopia Protection Cluster protection analysis noted:

‘Increasing fuel shortages, liquidity constraints, and inflation are emerging as significant drivers of protection risks across Ethiopia, affecting civilian access to essential services, livelihoods, and humanitarian assistance. Rising fuel prices and reduced availability have increased cost of transportation and essential items, constrained movement, disrupted supply chains, and affected the delivery of life-saving assistance, with disproportionate impacts on women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, and those in remote or displacement-affected areas. In Tigray, where fuel supplies have been severely disrupted since early 2026, black-market fuel prices exceeded ETB 800 (approximately USD 5) [£3.71[footnote 44]] per litre, contributing to the suspension of 148 humanitarian interventions across 84 woredas, affecting approximately 1.8 million people. Fuel shortages have also constrained ambulance services, health facility operations, water trucking, telecommunications, and access and protection monitoring in hard-to-reach communities …

‘Cash liquidity challenges have further compounded vulnerabilities, limiting households’ ability to meet basic needs and reducing the effectiveness of cash-based humanitarian assistance. In Tigray, cash shortages and limited liquidity in banks and ATMs have constrained the delivery of humanitarian cash assistance. Across affected areas, reduced purchasing power and disrupted access to markets have increased reliance on harmful coping mechanisms, including child labour, early marriage, exploitation, and negative survival strategies. These constraints are weakening community protection mechanisms, limiting safe access to services, and increasing protection risks.’[footnote 45]

4.2 Forced population displacement

4.2.1 A June 2025 report by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) stated that as of January 2025, there were an estimated 710,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Tigray and a further 40,000 in the Contested Areas - zone 2 (Mai Tsebri and surrounding areas) and zone 3 (Alamata and surrounding areas)[footnote 46].

4.2.2 A December 2025 UNICEF report noted:

‘In Tigray, living conditions for displaced populations remain dire and have worsened due to reduced humanitarian presence, funding shortages, and pipeline breaks. More than 740,000 people remain displaced, nearly 80 percent originating from contested areas between Amhara and Tigray. To address internal displacement, UNICEF launched the Multisectoral IDP Return Support Plan for Tigray in October 2025, supporting the Government of Ethiopia to facilitate the voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable return of an estimated 574,000 IDPs …to areas of origin in Western Tigray. No large‑scale movements back to areas of origin have occurred due to a range of persisting constraints.’[footnote 47]

4.2.3 The Global Protection Cluster February 2026 monthly overview reported the displacement of an estimated 2,500 people in the North Western and another 37,000 people in South Eastern Tigray. According to the report around 30,000 people of those displaced returned to their areas of origin, while around 7,000 remained displaced and were reported to be in urgent need of assistance[footnote 48].

4.2.4 On 27 April 2026, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) reported that renewed hostilities in Alamata, Raya Alamata and Raya Bala (Southern Tigray) in February 2026 led to the displacement of an estimated 78,450 people[footnote 49].

4.2.5 The United Nations Higher Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) reported that as of 31 July 2026, there were 761,284 IDPs in Tigray which represented 39.7% of total IDP population in Ethiopia which was estimated at 1,919,993. Of the IDP population in Tigray, 309,906 (40.7%) originated from North Western Tigray, 196,229 (25.8%) from Central Tigray and 116,571 (15.3%) from Mekelle[footnote 50]. A UNHCR update indicated that the number of IDPs in Tigray had not changed as of 31 August 2026[footnote 51].

4.2.6 On 3 August 2026, the BBC reported that fighting between regional forces and the ENDF in Tigray had displaced civilians, with hundreds of people crossing into neighbouring Sudan[footnote 52]. The source did not provide an estimate of the total number of people displaced by the fighting.

4.3 IDP returns

4.3.1 In September 2025, the Global Protection Cluster reported that 12,155 displaced households, comprising 62,707 individuals, had returned to their areas of origin across six woredas in Tigray, reflecting ongoing self-organised returns by IDPs. However, the individual woreda figures provided in the same report total 52,707 people, comprising 638 in Irob, 1,189 in Gulomekada, 17,839 in Zala-Anbassa, 1,835 in Egela, 1,814 in Central Adiyabo and 29,392 in Tahtay Adiyabo[footnote 53]. The reason for the 10,000-person discrepancy between the reported overall total and the sum of the woreda figures is unclear.

4.3.2 In September 2026, UNHCR reported that, as of 31 July 2026, there were 1,123,137 IDP returnees in Tigray[footnote 54].

4.3.3 In February 2026, the Global Protection Cluster Ethiopia monthly report stated that 30,000 people displaced in February 2026 returned to their areas of origin[footnote 55].

4.3.4 In April 2026, HRW reported that the Ethiopian government continued to support the return of displaced persons to contested areas of Tigray, including Western Tigray. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stated in February 2026 that displaced persons should be able to return to their homes while disputes over the area’s status remained unresolved. The report further noted that the UN had initiated a plan with the Ethiopian government for possible returns to Western Tigray in 2025. However, according to HRW, previous returns to the contested areas of Raya and Tselemti in 2024 were affected by a lack of humanitarian assistance, insecurity and violence by armed groups, which resulted in further displacement[footnote 56].

4.4 Conditions in IDP settlements and for IDP returnees

4.4.1 An April 2025 report by IOM and Shelter Cluster noted:

‘The humanitarian situation in Tigray remains critical, with 760,406 IDPs still living in precarious conditions across various settlement options. While the overall number of displaced persons has not significantly increased, living conditions continue to deteriorate due to dwindling resources and overcrowding. Many IDPs who previously lived in rental homes within host communities are now being forced into already overcrowded collective centers as they can no longer afford rent.

‘According to DTM SA R37, the Northwestern Zone alone hosts 309,906 IDPs (40% of the total displacement in Tigray), while the Central Zone hosts 196,229 IDPs (25.7%). These two zones together account for nearly 506,000 displaced individuals, yet shelter capacity remains critically low.

‘The strain on collective centers, particularly schools, remains a critical concern. EHF multisectoral funding, complemented by IOM shelter item donations, has enabled the relocation of IDPs from 21 schools. However, 92 schools across the region continue to house displaced families, with 67% located in the Northwest and Central Zones.

‘In addition to poor living conditions, the continued use of schools as shelters is severely disrupting education, leaving thousands of children unable to attend classes and further exacerbating the crisis. This situation is also straining relationships between the host community and IDPs, as local residents face disruptions to essential services, particularly education.’

‘Displaced families in sites such as May Hanse, Hitsats, Adi Mahameday, Adi Nebried, Tahtay Adiyabo, and all collective centers in Shire are living in unsafe, unplanned, and deteriorating conditions. Overcrowding has reached alarming levels, and shelters are collapsing under the pressure of continuous new arrivals.

‘In Endabaguna Collective Center, more than five families are packed in to a single room or makeshift shelters that are at high risk of collapse with no privacy and little protection from the elements. Meanwhile, in May Hanse, newly arrived IDPs are forced to erect ad hoc shelters and improvise sleeping arrangements due to a severe lack of household essentials. Basic items such as mattresses, blankets, and cooking supplies remain scarce.

‘In Adi Mahameday and Tahtay Adiyabo, the constant influx of new arrivals has overwhelmed the available space, pushing displaced families into even more precarious living conditions. The already limited resources are being stretched beyond capacity, worsening sanitation and exposing IDPs to greater health and protection risks.’[footnote 57]

4.4.2 A 2026 UNICEF humanitarian action appeal for Ethiopia noted:

‘In Tigray, the projected return of more than 500,000 people to their places of origin in Western Tigray will take place in a context of severely disrupted basic services. Hundreds of thousands of internally displaced persons remain in overcrowded camps with limited access to essential services, and the situation in Western Tigray remains particularly complex and sensitive. Adults and children with disabilities in Ethiopia face heightened vulnerabilities due to stigma, discrimination and limited access to services. The 2025 national disability survey found that 20 per cent of households include a person with a disability, with the highest prevalence in Tigray (30 per cent).’[footnote 58]

4.4.3 In August 2025, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) assessed the household needs among internally displaced persons (IDPs) in contested areas zone 1 (Humera and surrounding areas), zone 2 (Mai Tsabeli and surrounding areas) and zone 3 (Alamata and surrounding areas). In March 2026, IOM published 2 snapshot reports setting out the findings, one covering zone 1[footnote 59] and the other covering zones 2 and 3[footnote 60].

4.4.4 A March 2026 IOM household needs assessment of IDPs in Tigray, conducted in August 2025, found that:

The three most reported needs were access to food (96.0%), access to water (52.4%) and non-food items, specifically bedding sets (44.5%).

4.4.5 In March 2026, UNHCR published 2 reports on protection monitoring and solutions assessments conducted in Sheraro woreda, Northwestern Tigray and Adigrat woreda, Eastern Tigray. 4.4.6 Regarding Sheraro woreda, UNHCR reported that, of the basic facilities recorded in the areas visited, including schools, health centres, markets and civil registration offices, 16.7% were fully damaged and 8.3% were partially damaged[footnote 62]. 4.8 Access to WASH

4.8.1 The IFRC October 2026 report noted that drought had resulted in the drying of water points in affected areas, including parts of Tigray, creating risks for both people and livestock. Across the affected regions, more than 319 water points were either completely or partially dried out. However, the report did not disaggregate this figure by region and therefore did not specify how many of the affected water points were in Tigray[footnote 107].

4.8.2 According to EDHS 2024/2025 report 54% of the population in Tigray has access to at least basic drinking water services, slightly below the national average (57%) but higher than in Afar (30%), South West Ethiopia (38%), and Somali (40%). However, access remains constrained by service quality and availability: 17.8% of the population rely on limited services, 24.8% on unimproved sources, and 3% on surface water. In addition, 73.2% of households do not have drinking water on their premises and only 63.5% reported having sufficient drinking water available during the previous month, compared with 68% nationally[footnote 108]. Sanitation indicators in Tigray are substantially worse than national averages. Nationally, 31% of the population has access to at least basic sanitation services, while in Tigray only 10.4% use basic sanitation facilities. A further 17.0% rely on shared improved facilities, 7.8% use unimproved sanitation, and 64.8% practise open defecation[footnote 109].

6. Freedom of movement

6.1.1 HRW reported in April 2026 that freedom of movement for Tigrayans in Western Tigray remained restricted. According to HRW, Tigrayans were required to obtain temporary travel permits from local authorities to travel outside their immediate locality, including for employment, medical treatment and family visits. HRW stated that permits were generally limited in duration and geographical scope, with travel documents reviewed by the organisation indicating that movement outside authorised areas could result in prosecution. The report also described the presence of official and ad hoc checkpoints operated by security forces, where individuals were reportedly required to present identification documents or travel permits. HRW further reported that some interviewees limited their movements because of concerns about arrest, detention or harassment. The organisation contrasted these accounts with testimony from an Amhara resident who reported being able to travel without significant difficulty, including when not carrying identification documents[footnote 130].

6.1.2 On 20 April 2026, Ethiopia Today, citing reporting by Wazema, reported restrictions on the movement of young people attempting to leave Tigray. According to the source, authorities had established checkpoints on routes leading to the Amhara and Afar regions, where vehicles carrying groups of young people were reportedly intercepted and turned back. The same source reported that the Tigray Police Commission stated that it had intercepted and returned more than 150 people in one week and that 171 individuals had been detained while attempting to leave the region. According to the report some people sought to avoid checkpoints by travelling on foot and that individuals apprehended while attempting to leave at night were reportedly held in temporary detention facilities. The source stated that concerns about recruitment by Tigrayan forces and fears of renewed conflict were among the reasons cited by some young people for leaving the region[footnote 131].

6.1.3 An August 2026 Ethiopia Protection Cluster analysis reported that, across conflict affected and environmentally fragile areas of Ethiopia, checkpoints, insecurity along transport routes, armed actors, explosive ordnance contamination and localised restrictions limited civilians’ freedom of movement and their ability to access livelihoods, essential services and humanitarian assistance. Some communities also reported harassment, intimidation, extortion and arbitrary restrictions while travelling. 6.1.4 On 23 September 2026 Ethiopia Today reported that Ethiopian Airlines had cancelled scheduled flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire[footnote 133]. AP also reported that air travel to Tigray had been suspended after TPLF-affiliated fighters reportedly seized Mekelle airport, leading Ethiopian Airlines to cancel flights to and from the region[footnote 134].

EHRC also reported that the complete closure of land routes linking Tigray with other parts of Ethiopia restricted freedom of movement, disrupted the supply of basic goods and services, and contributed to subsequent price inflation[footnote 135].

6.1.6 A 25 September 2026 press release by the OHCHR stated: ‘Internet and telecommunication have reportedly been disrupted or are non-functional in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, and in parts of Amhara, and roads have reportedly been blocked in parts of Afar. Air travel has been significantly affected in Tigray after Ethiopian Airlines flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire were suspended following the TPLF’s takeover of all three airports on 23 September.’[footnote 136]

6.1.7 On 16 October 2026, Addis Standard reported that the TPLF warned civilians against movement around airports in Tigray, alleging that the federal government was using airport facilities for military purposes. The TPLF also warned against travelling to areas where the Tigray army was operating without its permission[footnote 137]
